title: The Price of Prestige
subtitle: CMPT 376W | G1 - ACM Code of Ethics Case Study | Group 15
scenario: Diane, a new graduate, joins a prestigious augmented reality research team. Its technical lead, Max, humiliates staff over mistakes, while research manager Jean protects his reputation and the funding he attracts. A tracking defect before a sponsor demonstration tests Diane's willingness to seek review. When Max removes Diane and coworker Eli from a paper that uses their work, she must balance earned credit, financial stability, Eli's wishes, and institutional accountability. HR adviser Priya explains possible responses without promising a finding. Four decision stages lead to five outcomes that preserve both gains and unresolved costs.
characters: A new graduate who values learning, rent-paying stability, and fair recognition. The player chooses her response to humiliation, the defect, research credit, and the future. Her technical responsibility does not make her responsible for Max's abusive choices.

An acclaimed AR researcher who equates deadlines and prestige with authority. He insults Diane, blames Eli, and uses authorship as punishment. His expertise explains his power without excusing the abuse. He directly responds to technical and credit decisions.

Fears losing funding and irreplaceable technical leadership. On the Jean route she dismisses Diane's concern; on every route she is copied on the credit decision. She acknowledges a written objection only if Diane sends one, and permits peer practices for productivity while protecting Max.

Wants reliable work and earned credit but fears retaliation. He reviews the defect with Diane when asked, explains the costs of secrecy or public blame, and voices his own reporting boundaries. After paired review he may authorize a specific named statement; Diane can still choose to leave it private.

Works outside Jean's reporting line and explains this fictional company's review, interim support, and transfer options. She distinguishes an options conversation from a formal report, accepts Diane's own observations without requiring Eli's participation, and cannot guarantee secrecy or a particular finding.
dilemmas: Speak up, document, or protect an immediate position

Tell Jean to seek supervisory intervention, even though Diane risks dismissal of her concern; record the incident while fresh to preserve a specific factual account, although a record alone brings no immediate protection; or remain quiet for now because Diane needs the job and fears becoming a target. The merged Defect scene remembers which response occurred. Only Record creates the contemporaneous outburst note.
Reliable review under fear of blame

Ask Eli to review and test a fix together because his expertise may expose a faulty assumption; this costs a morning and builds trust. Attempt a rushed solo repair to avoid exposing Eli or missing the deadline; inadequate review causes a reset regression, followed by rollback, a reviewed correction, and a two-day delay. Raise the defect openly to make the risk visible; Max targets Eli, while the team performs a focused review and delays a day. Reporting a defect never makes Diane responsible for Max's abuse.
Earned credit, another person's agency, and career security

Challenge the author list with permitted contribution records to defend recognition, despite further hostility. Alternatively, support Eli privately and ask what he wants shared: after Pair he permits a named statement for Priya, and Diane can accept that scope or leave him to send it himself; after Solo or Open he declines a statement. Accept the omission for now to avoid confrontation and preserve a reference or paycheque. Support is not evidence collection, and Eli's refusal does not stop Diane reporting her own experience.

File a factual formal report to seek external review of the management chain; its outcome depends on the authored information route and can remain unresolved. Request a transfer to protect well-being while giving up the prestigious research post; optionally leave an account of Diane's own experience, without treating it as a formal complaint. Stay and build peer review and a contribution ledger to improve what coworkers can control, while leadership remains unresolved. Keep working without further action to preserve immediate stability, leaving fear and unfair credit in place. None of these choices transfers responsibility for abuse from Max to Diane.
goals: Compare fixing the calibration labels and reviewing the tracker with Max's attacks on a person's worth. The correction is needed; humiliation is not. Ask what useful feedback would have sounded like in Outburst or Solo.
Compare self-protection, support, and reporting under uncertainty
Contrast Report, Exit, Peers, and Silence. Consider what each preserves and leaves unresolved, and why Eli's statement is voluntary. The endings invite reflection rather than awarding a moral score.
Explain why mistakes do not cancel earned research credit

Credit uses the same contributions after both competent review and a rushed error. Challenge records an objection; E1 restores credit while E3-E5 can leave the old paper unresolved. A contribution is not a reward for obedience.
Explain leadership's effect on working conditions and quality
Connect fear-driven secrecy in Solo with review and learning in Pair and Peers. Jean's incentives protect Max, while E4 shows that local technical gains do not establish institutional accountability.
outcomes: An independent review restores earned credit and an experienced interim supervisor handles daily reviews. The milestone moves and trust remains damaged. Eli's authorized statement can corroborate the account; without it, the dated note plus written objection leads to a separate confirming interview with Jean. ACM 1.5, 3.3, 3.4.

Interviews conflict and some colleagues will not speak on the record. The author list remains under review; an outside supervisor provides interim distance while Diane keeps her salary. Unresolved does not mean false. ACM 1.2, 3.4.

A transfer follows a two-week handover, preserving salary while costing the particular research opportunity. A voluntary exit account may be retained; it does not trigger a promised full review. Max still leads the old group. ACM 1.2, 3.3.
Peer review catches a later error and a contribution ledger improves traceability. The old credit dispute and Max's authority persist; people still tense when he enters. ACM 2.4, 2.6, 3.3, 3.4.

The sponsor demo succeeds using a reviewed repair, with the route's stated delay. Funding and pay continue while unfair credit and fear remain. Earlier challenge or support changes the personal consequence. ACM 1.4, 1.5.
